`git rebase --onto` lets you choose exactly which commits to move and where to put them. A plain `git rebase` only lets you pick the destination.

### Syntax

```
git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> [<branch>]
```

Git takes the commits that are in `<branch>` but not in `<upstream>`, which is the range `upstream..branch`, and replays them on top of `<newbase>`. `<upstream>` is exclusive: commits up to and including it are left behind. If you leave out `<branch>`, it uses the current branch.

### Example: move a branch off another feature branch

You branched `feature-b` off `feature-a`, but `feature-b` doesn't actually depend on `feature-a`. You want it based on `main`:

```
main:       A---B
                 \
feature-a:        C---D
                       \
feature-b:              E---F
```

```bash
git rebase --onto main feature-a feature-b
```

This means: take the commits in `feature-b` that aren't in `feature-a` (E and F) and replay them onto `main`:

```
main:       A---B
                |\
feature-a:      | C---D
                 \
feature-b:        E'---F'
```

C and D stay on `feature-a` only. A plain `git rebase main` run from `feature-b` would have carried them along too.

### Another common use: dropping commits

To remove commits from the middle of a branch, for example dropping C and D from `A-B-C-D-E` (with E as HEAD):

```bash
git rebase --onto B D
```

This replays everything after D (just E) onto B, giving `A-B-E'`.

The replayed commits get new hashes. If the branch was already pushed, you'll need to `git push --force-with-lease`.
